newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, U.S. row over reported snub of Christopher.
newsitem.headline: France, U.S. row over reported snub of Christopher.

text.p: Frayed relations between France and the United States hit another low on Friday after a tiff broke out over a purported snub by French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette of his outgoing U.S. counterpart Warren Christopher.
The row emerged on Thursday when the Washington Post reported de Charette had walked out during a toast in honour of Christopher at a NATO function in Brussels earlier in the week.

French President Jacques Chirac, who likes to refer to his affection for the United States dating back to his days as a student in Cambridge, Massachusetts, made no mention of the incident during a long television interview in Paris.
But explaining why France must back a common European currency, he said that "when it exists, it will allow us to fight efficiently against American hegemony."
Paris, backed by NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, had initially denied outright there was any substance to the story of the Brussels incident.
But the U.S. State department later confirmed the American press account and a U.S. official said de Charette had been "extremely discourteous."
De Charette's office then took a new tack and said he had not deliberately snubbed Christopher. A senior French official told Reuters that Solana's tribute had not been on the agenda.

The official said other prominent NATO foreign ministers had also been absent but he declined to identify them. De Charette, unaware of the tribute, had left the room to address a news conference, the official said.

The controversy reflected the raw state of Franco-U.S. relations, with disputes accumulating over the reform of NATO's military structure, the succession to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, France's drive for a bigger say in the Middle East and sharp diffrences over Western policy on Zaire.

The Post quoted an unnamed senior U.S. official as saying: "It was an incredible display of petulant behaviour. Everybody knows there are tensions in the French-American relationship, but nobody expects them to be shown at a personal level."

De Charette had initially called the report a "manipulation" and his spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt branded it an "ill-intentioned lie" aimed at damaging already frayed ties between Paris and Washington.

Paris and Washington frequently find themselves at odds on key global issues, but diplomats say Franco-American ties appear at a new low ebb despite a warm personal relationship between President Bill Clinton and Chirac.
Probably the most serious fight concerns the future of NATO's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean.

In what has been dubbed the battle for Naples, France is demanding that Washington hand over the post it has held since NATO was created in 1949 to a European. The United States has flatly refused and is not amenable to compromise. at the NATO hall."

The latest row took place after all U.N. Security Council members except France voted for Kofi Annan, the international body's undersecretary-general for peacekeeping, to replace current secretary-general Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Paris campaigned Boutros-Ghali's reappointment but Washington backs the Ghanaian.
